records.title: “To Save Our Brethren”: Mormons, Armenians, and the “Eastern Zion” in Ottoman Palestine and Beyond
records.abstract: On October 13, 1897, Mormon church leaders reached a consensus to establish a “colony in Palestine.”1 It was a major decision. After thirteen years of missionary work, some two hundred Armenian adults and children had congregated in four branches in Aleppo (northern Syria), Aintab and Marash (southern Turkey), and Zara (east-central Turkey). These converts faced daily, intense persecution in their homeland due to their conversion to an “alien” faith. They were thwarted from emigrating to be with the Saints in America because of their poverty and the hostility of both American and Ottoman officials. In view of the desperate straits of these Armenian Mormons, the church leaders proposed an “Eastern Zion.” They dispatched a high-level delegation, including Apostle Anthon Lund, former Turkish Mission President Ferdinand Hintze, and Hagop Gagosian, an Armenian convert who had emigrated from Turkey to Utah, to determine a site for an agricultural colony, negotiate terms for the purchase of land, obtain formal permission for the gathering and resettlement of the Armenian congregations, and offer an apostolic benediction on the land.2The envoys left Utah on January 6, 1898, visiting Mormon communities and missionaries in the eastern United States and Europe. They debarked at Jaffa, in Ottoman Palestine on February 17, 1898.3 Phillip Maycock and Andrew Larson, the two missionaries then working in the Turkish Mission, greeted them. Together, the members of the delegation began their work.Though the number of Armenian Saints was small compared to other Mormon missionary fields, the story of the 1898 Mormon delegation provides important information to understand deeply held beliefs about time, place, and peoples at a pivotal moment in the church's history. The story also reveals the lengths significant religious actors would go to reshape doctrinal beliefs and attitudes to assist a beleaguered community of fellow church members in a distant empire.To determine how to set up a colony, the Mormon delegation explored similar settlements in Ottoman Palestine. The first day, they visited the German “Templer settlement.” A small evangelical German Lutheran group, inspired by their reading of biblical prophetic passages, the Templers had started a “perfect” Christian community in Haifa in preparation for Christ's Second Coming. The Mormon group then took the land route northward toward Haifa. They stopped at the Jewish settlements of Haderah and “Sammarin” (Zikhron Ya'akov) to examine agricultural efforts. In Haderah, the Mormons met with Selig Soskin, a Russian-born, German-trained agronomist who had emigrated to Palestine two years earlier and was working for the Palestine Executive of the Odessa Committee of Hovevei Zion.4 Lund reported obtaining “much valuable information” from “the Doctor” on land reclamation, property and produce taxes, livestock and cereals, and eucalyptus tree planting as an anti-malarial measure. He was “glad to have taken that route,” visiting “the Jewish colonies” and learning from Soskin “considerable information in regard to what they had done and the resources of the country.”5 The group then visited the “American colony” in Jerusalem. Founded by Horatio and Anna Spafford in 1881, there were 150 American and Swedish members by 1896 dedicated to non-proselytizing, philanthropic work in Jerusalem. Lund praised their cooperative spirit. These settlements played a key role in making Mormon arguments for a “colony” of Armenian Saints plausible.Earlier Mormon missionaries had visited other colony settlements from 1884 to 1898 while touring throughout Palestine. They “traveled from colony to colony”—both Jewish and Christian—and, in some cases, published extensive descriptions of their experiences.6 For example, Danish convert and missionary Janne Sjodahl wrote articles for the Deseret News Weekly divided into sections entitled “Objects of Jewish Colonization,” “Colonization Methods,” “Colonial Life,” “Religious Notions and Education,” and “Non-Colonizing Jews.”7 He compared Jewish and “Gentile” agricultural colonies and noted the transitions underway in Jewish settlements. He remarked on the “inviting appearance” of Petah Tikveh, Rosh Pinah, and “Samarin” (Zikhron Ya'akov), observing: “It is very pleasing to me to note . . . on the progress everywhere going on. . . . The Jews are settling to stay.”8Sjodahl and other Mormon missionaries noted the number of settlers, the types and arrangementsof buildings, enterprises, crops, livestock, and cultivation methods. Sjodahl explained, “These people have fully demonstrated what diligence and skill can do here. They have bought up some desert lands . . . have terraced mountains . . . laid out the land in vineyards, and they are obtaining fair returns from their labor.”9 These descriptions and assessments helped the 1898 delegates lay out plans for establishing a Mormon colony. They also contributed to the Mormons’ positive regard for modern Zionist settlements and ideology during the Ottoman and British Mandate periods.10Those who wrote these descriptions of potential Palestine settlements drew upon their experiences in Utah. In the last decades of the nineteenth century, Mormon leaders remained keen proponents of agricultural colonization efforts carried out by church members for economic, social, and cultural reasons.11 The proposal to settle urban Armenians alongside a small number of European and American Mormons assigned by church headquarters to colonize according to up-to-date agrarian and industrial skills drew upon longstanding experience in the American West; it also rose from deep seated convictions about the necessity for the in-gathering of the Saints before the “coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.”12With this background, Hintze and other missionaries sought official recognition (millet status) for the Mormon community in Ottoman domains.13 They met with U.S. and European consular agents for advice and information,14 consulted with Armenian converts,15 and upon returning to Mormon church headquarters in Utah, met with church leaders to enlist their support.16After visiting colony examples, Lund and the rest of the delegation traveled by steamship, carriage, and horseback to Aintab (Gaziantep), Turkey, site of the largest Mormon Armenian community, in March 1898.17 Lund's delegation ministered to the Saints for a month. They viewed and heard first-hand graphic examples of faithfulness and of anxieties, of the indigence of church members and the indignities imposed on those who converted to the new religion. For example, members recollected how “they had a hard time finding work because they were Mormons. [We] were the first ones fired and the last ones hired.” “We tried to hold meetings, which was difficult,” said George Z. Aposhian, “but we held them for several years. As members, we would go to church [and] people would stand on the side of the road and throw sticks and stones. . . . This went on for quite some time.”18The delegation then held two major council sessions to introduce the proposed colony. Most members, however, preferred emigrating to Utah. But they recognized the American and Ottoman travel restrictions, as well as their own poverty as prohibitive. So the delegation persuaded them to back the colony scheme. However, the Armenian Saints insisted that “light industry”—that is, weaving and rug making—be an essential part of the colony plan since most of the male church members were weavers, dyers, and rug makers and not experienced farmers. Moses Hindoian, of the Aintab branch, for example, “made his living by spinning and weaving wool. Everyone helped, even the children. So [his son] Abraham started working with wool . . . in his early years.”19 The Armenians also advised the Americans on prudent land purchase approaches and securing ownership titles.20After these meetings, the delegation traveled through “all the principal part of Palestine”21 in April and May 1898. During this period, they met with American consular officials in Beirut and Jerusalem, Turkish and Arab landowners and their agents, and German and Jewish settlers. They visited historic sites and surveyed a number of properties available for purchase. While they discussed sites near Nablus and Jericho as possessing great potential for agricultural settlement,22 it was the property near Haifa owned by Selim Khouri, a businessman and sometimes Russian and Greek charge d’ affaires, that seized their interest.23 It was a six thousand acre site about fifteen miles southeast of Haifa—the village and land of “El Kireh.” Though Khouri's asking price was $120,000, the envoys recommended it to general church officials in Utah for purchase and settlement.24The delegation's accounts matched historical geographer Ruth Kark's observations about “trends and processes connected with land and settlement” during this period.25 Mormons noted “the long term neglect” of once fertile and populated lands.26 They reported extensive tracts available for purchase by foreigners.27 They worried about the unsettled nature of occupancy rights versus land titles possessed and sold by absentee landowners.28 Discussions between Mormons, American consuls, and land agents show that Ottoman officials and merchant families in Beirut and Jaffa were deeply involved in speculative land ownership and that many of them sought avidly to realize profits on land sales to foreign buyers.29The Mormons were also part of a trend in the late 1880s and 1890s. Overriding ideological, rather than entrepreneurial, interest motivated land purchase and settlement in Ottoman Palestine.30 The delegation were there to “see our Zion . . . here” and save their Armenian fellow Saints.31 They feared displacing fellahin from Khouri's lands and occasionally asked “where the Son of man has been.”32 The goal of the Mormon colony was to create an economically self-sustaining refuge for the Saints, an enclave of “true arts” and “civilization” which would serve as a refuge from persecution and, in the interim, as a “city on the hill in the ‘East,’” even as Mormons hoped their settlement in the semi-arid valleys of the Rocky Mountains would serve as a sanctuary in the “latter-days” before the Lord's Second Advent.Land agents and owners told the Mormons repeatedly that they “could get anything they wanted” in the way of property, and in “any amount,” even if it meant driving its inhabitants off the land. This showed the uncertainties of the Ottoman agrarian classes and the impunity of their overlord's use of power.33 The Mormon delegation observed tax conscriptees working fitfully and fruitlessly on a road project that led nowhere. They noted villages emptied of adult men hiding from tax assessors which pointed to nagging treasury shortfalls and a decaying infrastructure.34 The Mormons wrote about Circassian immigrants, displaced by Ottoman defeats to Russia in the 1860s-1870s, wasting away in Palestinian villages beset by malaria and the absence of capital to improve the land which also hinted at the enormity of an Ottoman of the and land purchase Jews and Armenians and the about land the of European and upon Ottoman was as to as that of the and a the Armenian were and was and economically throughout the Ottoman the Ottoman in the and from European had rights to the Armenian Armenian inspired by in and to establish an Armenian in eastern and Armenian with Ottoman in several eastern and and in the capital of an Armenian of a of of Armenians the to create on the were to Ottoman in Mormon Ferdinand Hintze told the land and in Beirut who had about Jews to purchase lands of Mormon to settle Armenians in the was and is an They be and of the late Ottoman have pointed to the between and versus the of and with regard to land sales in Palestine. records.title: Compulsory Schooling Reforms and Fertility in Europe
records.abstract: We study the relationship between education and fertility, ex-ploiting compulsory schooling reforms in Europe as source of exogenous variation in education. Using data from 8 European countries, we assess the causal effect of education on the num-ber of biological kids and the incidence of childlessness. We find that more education causes a substantial decrease in child-lessness and an increase in the average number of children per woman. Our findings are robust to a number of falsification checks and we can provide complementary empirical evidence on the mechanisms leading to these surprising results. JEL: I2, J13

records.title: The Effect of Education on Fertility: Evidence from a Compulsory Schooling Reform
records.abstract: This study analyzes the effect of education on the number of children, childlessness, and the timing of births. We use exogenous variation from a mandatory reform of compulsory schooling in West Germany to deal with the endogeneity of schooling. In contrast to studies for other developed countries, we find a significant negative effect of education on fertility. This negative effect seems to operate mainly through a postponement of first births away from the teenage years. In addition, education reduces the probability of first motherhood among women in their early 30s. We attribute these findings to the particularly high opportunity costs of child-rearing in Germany.

Do Compulsory Schooling Laws Affect Fertility Behaviors and Marriages? Evidence From India
records.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper exploits an education policy in India generated by a 2010 schooling reform to examine the effect of education on women's family planning decisions. The key element of the reform was that it required students to complete 8 years of primary education (age 6–14 years). I employ an instrumental variable difference‐in‐difference approach that measures the exogenous variation in treatment intensity in different states across birth cohorts of women measured by birth year and birth month. The reform led to an increase in total years of education, a delay in the age at first marriage, a postponement of sexual activity, and reduced fertility beginning at the age of 23. I also examine the potential mechanisms through which increased education affects fertility. The findings suggest that early use of modern contraceptives, reduction in the marital education gap, increased literacy, and utilization of healthcare services contribute to reduced fertility. These results are consistent with the increased empowerment of women influencing their fertility decisions, highlighting the importance of the government's efforts to promote education through policy initiatives.

records.title: Compulsory Education and Fertility over the Life Cycle – Evidence from a Natural Experiment
records.venue: The B E Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy
records.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the effect of compulsory education on women’s fertility over the reproductive life cycle, exploiting the 1972 compulsory schooling reform in Britain. Using data from the General Household Survey and a regression discontinuity design, the study finds that exposure to the reform is associated with a reduction of about 0.09 children for women observed at ages 20–30, but an increase of about 0.31 children for women observed at ages 40 and above. The pattern is consistent with a life-cycle interpretation in which compulsory education is associated with lower cumulative fertility at earlier stages but higher fertility accumulation at later stages of the reproductive life cycle. Overall, the findings indicate that education-induced reductions in early-life fertility need not translate into lower cumulative fertility observed at older ages.

records.title: Books or babies? Incapacitation and human capital effects of extended compulsory schooling on the teenage fertility of ethnic minority women
records.abstract: This paper examines the effects of an increase in the compulsory school-leaving (CSL) age on the teenage fertility of Roma women, a disadvantaged ethnic minority in Hungary. We use a regression discontinuity design (RDD) identification strategy and show that raising the CSL age from 16 to 18 decreased the probability of teenage motherhood among Roma women by 6.8 percentage points and delayed early motherhood by two years. We contribute to the literature by exploiting a database that covers live births, miscarriages, abortions, and still births, and contains information on the time of conception precise to the week to separate the incapacitation and human capital effects of education on fertility. We find that higher CSL age decreases the probability of getting pregnant during the school year but not during summer and Christmas breaks, which suggests that the estimated effects are generated mostly through the incapacitation channel.
